scenario.su: A student must decide whether a recorded feature shows list writing, direct element access, or iteration through a list. The label must match the named feature despite nearby observations describing the other list relations.
scenario.ma: Students compare square-bracket notation [] holding comma-separated values, an observation of direct access using an index, a for-loop observation of each element visited in order.

mc.q: A student compares square brackets holding comma-separated values with an index used on an individual element. Which distinction matches the observed list notation and access?
op: Square brackets write lists; indexes access elements
Indexes write lists; square brackets access elements
Lists write indexes; elements access square brackets
Elements write square brackets; lists access indexes
mc.ex: A list is written with square brackets holding comma-separated values, while an index directly accesses an individual element. Assigning list writing to indexes reverses these distinct relations.

mc.q: A student observes an index selecting an individual element and a for loop visiting each element in order. Which account fits both observations?
op: An index accesses elements; a for loop iterates
A for loop accesses elements; an index iterates
Elements access indexes; a for loop iterates
A list accesses indexes; elements visit a for loop
mc.ex: An index directly accesses an individual element, and a for loop iterates through a list in element order. Saying the for loop performs direct indexed access swaps the supplied roles.

keyTerms.df: The index of an element within a list is a numerical position that starts at zero and increases sequentially.
keyTerms.eg: Individual elements are accessed directly using an index, such as accessing the first element at index 0.

keyTerms.cx: A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order.

scenario.su: A programmer needs to process a sequence of student scores stored in a list, but they must ensure every score is examined exactly once. The constraint is that the list contains exactly five scores, and the processing must occur in the exact sequence the scores were entered.

mc.q: When accessing the third element of a list, which statement correctly describes the index starting point and the access method?
op: Accessing the third element uses index 3 because indexes start at one.
Accessing the third element uses index 2 because indexes begin at zero.
Accessing the third element requires a for loop to visit the element.
Accessing the third element uses the list's length minus one as the index.
mc.ex: A list is written with square brackets [] holding comma-separated values, and indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence, which supports the second option, while the first option incorrectly states indexes start at one.

mc.q: Given the list [10, 20, 30], if a for loop is used to visit each element in order, what is the correct sequence of elements visited?
op: The loop visits 10, 20, 30 in reverse order.
The loop visits 10, 20, 30 in the order they are stored.
The loop visits 10, 30, 20 because indexes start at zero.
The loop visits 20, 30, 10 because indexes begin at one.
mc.ex: A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order, which supports the second option, while the first option incorrectly suggests reverse order.

lessonInput.title: Electric current
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface. Claim 1: Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move. Claim 2: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

claims: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface.
Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.
Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

anchors.quote: electric current is the rate at which charge flows
direction of positive charge flow
constant velocity, known as the drift velocity

facts: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface.
Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.
Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

keyTerms.df: Electric current is a rate quantity defined by charge passing through a surface.
keyTerms.eg: Charge passes through a surface, and electric current reports the associated rate.
keyTerms.mi: Electric current names the surface through which charge passes.
keyTerms.cx: The surface marks where passage occurs; current describes the rate of that passage.

keyTerms.df: Conventional current direction identifies the direction in which positive charge would move.
keyTerms.eg: Positive charge would move in the conventional current direction.
keyTerms.mi: Conventional current direction is the rate at which positive charge passes.
keyTerms.cx: It specifies possible positive-charge motion in a direction rather than measuring passage rate.

keyTerms.df: Microscopic drift speed is slow compared with the rapidly propagating electric signal through a circuit.
keyTerms.eg: A circuit comparison pairs slow microscopic drift speed with rapid electric-signal propagation.
keyTerms.mi: Microscopic drift speed propagates rapidly while the electric signal is slow.
keyTerms.cx: The rapid propagation belongs to the electric signal, while microscopic drift remains slow.

scenario.su: A workshop group must assign accurate labels to four statements about charge, direction, drift speed, and signal propagation. The group faces a deadline and must distinguish the paired ideas using the stated observations rather than treating their properties as interchangeable.
scenario.ma: charge-through-surface rate notation, positive-charge direction notation, slow-drift observation, rapid-signal observation

mc.q: A comparison records charge passing through a surface at a rate and separately marks the direction positive charge would move. Which distinction correctly labels electric current and conventional current direction?
op: Current gives charge-passage rate; conventional direction tracks positive charge
Current tracks positive charge; conventional direction gives passage rate
Current gives positive-charge direction; conventional direction marks surface
Current marks the surface; conventional direction gives charge rate
mc.ex: Electric current is the rate of charge passing through a surface, whereas conventional current direction follows the direction positive charge would move. The two relations should not be exchanged between rate and direction.

mc.q: In a circuit comparison, the recorded microscopic drift speed is slow while the observed electric signal propagates rapidly. Under a constraint requiring one accurate paired label, which notation is supported?
op: Drift speed is slow; electric signal propagates rapidly
Drift speed is rapid; electric signal propagates slowly
Drift speed is rapid; electric signal propagates rapidly
Drift speed is slow; electric signal propagates slowly
mc.ex: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly. Rapid propagation therefore describes the signal, not the microscopic drift speed.

facts: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface.
Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.
Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

keyTerms.df: Electric current is defined as the rate at which charge passes through a surface.
keyTerms.eg: A flow of charge through a wire is measured by the current passing through a cross-section.
keyTerms.mi: Electric current is the speed at which charge moves through a wire.
keyTerms.cx: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface.

keyTerms.df: Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move through a circuit.
keyTerms.eg: If positive charges were moving, the current would be defined as flowing in that direction.
keyTerms.mi: Conventional current direction is the direction negative charge actually moves.
keyTerms.cx: Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.

keyTerms.df: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.
keyTerms.eg: The actual movement of charge carriers within a material is characterized by a slow drift speed.
keyTerms.mi: Microscopic drift speed is fast because the electric signal propagates rapidly.
keyTerms.cx: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

scenario.su: A technician measures the flow of charge through a copper wire and observes a signal propagating through the circuit very quickly. The technician must determine the correct direction of the current flow based on the movement of positive charge. The constraint is that the measurement must align with the definition of conventional current direction.
scenario.ma: The technician observes a current flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a battery. They compare this observation to a diagram showing the actual movement of electrons within the copper wire. The technician must decide which direction represents the conventional current flow.

mc.q: When analyzing a circuit, how does the conventional current direction relate to the actual movement of positive charge within the material?
op: Conventional current is the actual movement of positive charge.
Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move.
Conventional current is the speed of charge movement.
Conventional current is the rate of charge passing through a surface.
mc.ex: Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move, then conventional current is the direction positive charge would move.

mc.q: A circuit exhibits a very fast signal propagation, yet the microscopic drift speed of the charge carriers is slow; which statement accurately describes this relationship?
op: Drift speed is fast while signal propagation is slow.
Drift speed is slow even though signal propagation is rapid.
Drift speed is fast because the signal propagates rapidly.
Drift speed is slow because the signal propagates slowly.
mc.ex: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly, then drift speed is slow even though signal propagation is rapid.

lessonInput.title: While loops
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration. Claim 1: After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue. Claim 2: If the loop expression is true, the body runs again; if it is false, the loop terminates. Claim 3: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.
lessonInput.readings: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.1 While loop

claims: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.
After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.
If the loop expression is true, the body runs again; if it is false, the loop terminates.
A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.

anchors.quote: A while loop is a code construct that runs a set of statements, known as the loop body, while a given condition, known as the loop expression, is true
At each iteration, once the loop statement is executed, the loop expression is evaluated again
If true, the loop body will execute at least one more time. If false, the loop's execution will terminate
the loop body must make progress toward ending the condition

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.1 While loop

facts: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.
After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.
If the loop expression is true, the body runs again; if it is false, the loop terminates.
A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.

keyTerms.df: A while loop is a loop that re-checks its condition before each iteration while the condition stays true.
keyTerms.eg: The while loop body runs again when the loop condition is true.
keyTerms.mi: A while loop terminates when its loop condition is true.
keyTerms.cx: A true loop condition sends the body through another pass.

keyTerms.df: A loop condition is the expression whose result determines whether the body runs again or the loop terminates.
keyTerms.eg: The loop condition is true, so the body runs again.
keyTerms.mi: A false loop condition causes the body to run again.
keyTerms.cx: When that condition is false, the loop terminates.

keyTerms.df: An infinite loop is a loop whose condition never becomes false and therefore runs forever.
keyTerms.eg: After each pass, the loop expression is true and the body runs again.
keyTerms.mi: An infinite loop terminates while its expression stays true.
keyTerms.cx: A true expression continues the body instead of ending the loop.

scenario.su: A student must classify a while loop before a deadline by comparing a trace where the loop expression is true after each pass with a notation that the condition never becomes false. The body does not make progress toward ending the condition, but the student must decide whether the loop runs forever or terminates.
scenario.ma: condition notation: never becomes false, pass-by-pass observation: loop expression is true, body notation: does not make progress toward ending the condition

mc.q: A trace compares a true loop expression with a false loop expression; which distinction correctly predicts whether the body runs again or the loop terminates?
op: True reruns body; false terminates loop
True terminates loop; false reruns body
True reruns body; false reruns body
True terminates loop; false terminates loop
mc.ex: A true loop expression makes the body run again, while a false expression terminates the loop. The loop does not terminate when the expression is true.

mc.q: Before a deadline, a trace shows that the condition never becomes false and the body makes no progress toward ending it; which statement should the student select?
op: The loop runs forever
The loop terminates after another pass
The loop expression becomes false
The body makes progress toward ending
mc.ex: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever, matching the trace. It does not terminate after another pass while that condition remains true.

facts: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.
After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.
If the loop expression is true, the body runs again; if it is false, the loop terminates.
A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.

keyTerms.df: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.
keyTerms.eg: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.
keyTerms.mi: A while loop only checks its condition once before starting the body execution.
keyTerms.cx: The while loop re-checks the condition before each iteration, which is a necessary property for its operation.

keyTerms.df: After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.
keyTerms.eg: After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.
keyTerms.mi: The loop condition is only evaluated once at the very beginning of the loop.
keyTerms.cx: The loop expression is evaluated again after each pass through the body to decide whether to continue.

keyTerms.df: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.
keyTerms.eg: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.
keyTerms.mi: An infinite loop occurs when the loop condition is always true and the body does not change the condition.
keyTerms.cx: An infinite loop requires the body to make progress toward ending the condition, meaning the condition must eventually become false.

scenario.su: A program needs to process user input until a specific flag is set, requiring a while loop structure. The constraint is that the loop must terminate if the input is invalid, which means the condition must eventually become false.
scenario.ma: Compare the execution flow when the condition is initially true and the body modifies the condition versus when the condition is initially false and the body does not modify it.

mc.q: Distinguish between the repeated evaluation of the loop expression and the termination criteria of the while loop.
op: The loop expression is evaluated only once before the body starts.
The loop expression is evaluated again after each pass through the body.
The loop expression is evaluated only when the loop terminates.
The loop expression is evaluated only if the body executes successfully.
mc.ex: The loop expression is evaluated again after each pass through the body, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

mc.q: Given a while loop where the condition is always true, what must the body accomplish for the loop to eventually terminate?
op: The loop condition must remain true throughout execution.
The body must never execute any code.
The body must make progress toward ending the condition.
The loop condition must be explicitly set to false.
mc.ex: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

lessonInput.title: Strings and slicing
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A string is a sequence of characters indexed from left to right starting at 0; slicing extracts a contiguous substring with the [a:b] notation. Claim 1: For a string s, the left-most character is index 0 and the right-most is index len(s) - 1. Claim 2: Negative indexing refers to characters from right to left starting at -1. Claim 3: A slice s[a:b] returns characters from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive).
lessonInput.readings: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §1.4 String basics; §8.2 String slicing

claims: A string is a sequence of characters indexed from left to right starting at 0; slicing extracts a contiguous substring with the [a:b] notation.
For a string s, the left-most character is index 0 and the right-most is index len(s) - 1.
Negative indexing refers to characters from right to left starting at -1.
A slice s[a:b] returns characters from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive).

anchors.quote: A string is made up of a sequence of characters indexed from left to right, starting at 0
the left-most character is indexed 0 and the right-most character is indexed len(s) - 1
Negative indexing can also be used to refer to characters from right to left starting at -1
starting from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive) is returned

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §1.4 String basics; §8.2 String slicing

facts: A string is a sequence of characters indexed from left to right starting at 0; slicing extracts a contiguous substring with the [a:b] notation.
For a string s, the left-most character is index 0 and the right-most is index len(s) - 1.
Negative indexing refers to characters from right to left starting at -1.
A slice s[a:b] returns characters from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive).

keyTerms.df: A string belongs to the category of character sequences and has indexed characters.
keyTerms.eg: In string s, the left-most character has index 0.
keyTerms.mi: A string is indexed from right to left starting at 0.
keyTerms.cx: The starting side for index 0 is the left, not the right.

keyTerms.df: Slicing is extraction of a contiguous substring through the [a:b] notation.
keyTerms.eg: In s[a:b], a is inclusive and b is exclusive.
keyTerms.mi: Slicing with [a:b] includes the character at b.
keyTerms.cx: The substring stops before index b, so b is excluded.

keyTerms.df: Negative indexing is character reference from right to left, beginning at -1.
keyTerms.eg: In string s, index -1 starts from the right-most character.
keyTerms.mi: Negative indexing starts at 0 on the left.
keyTerms.cx: Its starting value is -1 on the right, not 0 on the left.

scenario.su: A student must classify two annotations for string s before a deadline. The student must distinguish character positions from slice boundaries while preserving the stated indexing directions.
scenario.ma: the annotation s[0] paired with the left-most character, the annotation s[-1] paired with the right-most character, the notation s[a:b] marking a inclusive and b exclusive

mc.q: A student compares the left-most character of string s with a character reached through Negative indexing. Which distinction matches the stated indexing directions and starting values?
op: Index len(s)-1 starts left; -1 starts left.
Index -1 starts left; 0 starts right.
Index 0 starts left; -1 starts right.
Index 0 starts right; -1 starts left.
mc.ex: The left-most character is index 0, while Negative indexing starts from the right at -1. Index -1 does not begin on the left, and index 0 does not begin on the right.

mc.q: For the notation s[a:b], a student observes the two boundary indexes but must decide before a deadline which boundary description matches the slice.
op: s[a:b] excludes a and includes b.
s[a:b] includes a and includes b.
s[a:b] excludes a and excludes b.
s[a:b] includes a and excludes b.
mc.ex: The slice begins with index a included and stops before index b. The boundary roles are not reversed: a is not excluded while b is included.

facts: A string is a sequence of characters indexed from left to right starting at 0; slicing extracts a contiguous substring with the [a:b] notation.
For a string s, the left-most character is index 0 and the right-most is index len(s) - 1.
Negative indexing refers to characters from right to left starting at -1.
A slice s[a:b] returns characters from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive).

keyTerms.df: A string is defined as a sequence of characters indexed from left to right starting at 0, which forms the fundamental structure for indexing operations.
keyTerms.eg: In the string 'Python', the character 'P' is at index 0 and 'n' is at index 1.
keyTerms.mi: A string is just a collection of characters without any defined order or starting point.
keyTerms.cx: The string is a sequence of characters indexed from left to right starting at 0, establishing a specific order and starting point for all character access.

keyTerms.df: Slicing extracts a contiguous substring from a string using the [a:b] notation to define the boundaries of the extracted segment.
keyTerms.eg: The slice 's[1:4]' on a string extracts characters starting at index 1 up to, but not including, index 4.
keyTerms.mi: Slicing is a method that modifies the original string by changing its underlying character sequence.
keyTerms.cx: Slicing extracts a contiguous substring with the [a:b] notation, which is a non-mutating operation that retrieves a segment.

keyTerms.df: Negative indexing refers to accessing characters within a string by counting from the right-most character, where -1 represents the last character.
keyTerms.eg: For a string of length 5, index -1 points to the fifth character, and -5 points to the first character.
keyTerms.mi: Negative indexing always starts counting from the left side of the string.
keyTerms.cx: Negative indexing refers to characters from right to left starting at -1, which is the specific mechanism for accessing elements from the end.

scenario.su: A data processing pipeline handles a user input string, 'DataBoundary', and needs to extract the middle segment for validation. The constraint is that the extraction must be done using only the defined slicing notation.
scenario.ma: Compare the result of s[0:4] and s[-4:] when s is 'DataBoundary'.

mc.q: When using the slice notation s[a:b], what is the relationship between the index 'a' and the character at that position?
op: Index a is the right-most character included in the result.
Index a is the character at the end of the result.
Index a is the character immediately preceding the end of the result.
Index a is the character immediately following the start of the result.
mc.ex: A slice s[a:b] returns characters from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive), so index a is the character immediately following the start of the result, correcting the option that suggests it is the right-most character included in the result.

mc.q: Given the string 'BoundaryTest', what is the result of the slice s[1:4] and why does it exclude the character at index 4?
op: The result is 'ound', excluding index 4 because the notation starts at index 4.
The result is 'ound', excluding index 4 because the notation is exclusive.
The result is 'ound', excluding index 4 because the notation is right-to-left.
The result is 'ound', excluding index 4 because the notation is inclusive.
mc.ex: A slice s[a:b] returns characters from index a (inclusive) up to index b (exclusive), so the result is 'ound', excluding index 4 because the notation is exclusive, correcting the option that suggests it is inclusive.

lessonInput.title: Plate-boundary processes
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Plate boundaries are classified as divergent, convergent, or transform according to whether plates separate, approach, or slide alongside one another. Claim 1: Divergent boundaries move apart and form new crust, whereas convergent boundaries move together and can subduct crust. Claim 2: Transform boundaries accommodate plates moving side by side rather than creating or subducting crust.
lessonInput.readings: Steven Earle, Physical Geology – 2nd Edition (2019), chapter 10 summary, BCcampus Open Education

claims: Plate boundaries are classified as divergent, convergent, or transform according to whether plates separate, approach, or slide alongside one another.
Divergent boundaries move apart and form new crust, whereas convergent boundaries move together and can subduct crust.
Transform boundaries accommodate plates moving side by side rather than creating or subducting crust.

anchors.quote: The three types of plate boundaries are divergent, convergent, and transform
divergent (plates moving apart and new crust forming), convergent (plates moving together and one being subducted)
transform (plates moving side by side)

attribution: Steven Earle, Physical Geology – 2nd Edition (2019), chapter 10 summary, BCcampus Open Education

facts: Plate boundaries are classified as divergent, convergent, or transform according to whether plates separate, approach, or slide alongside one another.
Divergent boundaries move apart and form new crust, whereas convergent boundaries move together and can subduct crust.
Transform boundaries accommodate plates moving side by side rather than creating or subducting crust.

keyTerms.df: Divergent describes boundaries where plates move apart and form new crust.
keyTerms.eg: A boundary where plates separate and new crust forms is divergent.
keyTerms.mi: A divergent boundary has plates moving together and subducting crust.
keyTerms.cx: Moving together and possible crust subduction identify convergent boundaries instead.

keyTerms.df: Convergent boundaries are plate boundaries that move together and can subduct crust.
keyTerms.eg: Plates approaching one another with crust subduction indicate convergent boundaries.
keyTerms.mi: Convergent boundaries accommodate plates sliding alongside one another.
keyTerms.cx: Side-by-side plate movement corresponds to transform boundaries rather than convergent boundaries.

keyTerms.df: Transform boundaries accommodate plates moving side by side rather than creating or subducting crust.
keyTerms.eg: Plates recorded as sliding alongside one another indicate transform boundaries.
keyTerms.mi: Transform boundaries move apart and form new crust.
keyTerms.cx: Plate separation with new crust formation corresponds to divergent boundaries instead.

scenario.su: A geologist must classify a boundary before review closes while colleagues dispute the divergent, convergent, and transform labels. The plate-motion notation shows side-by-side movement, and the crust record shows neither creation nor subduction.
scenario.ma: plate-motion notation showing side-by-side movement, crust record showing neither creation nor subduction, disputed divergent label, disputed transform label

mc.q: A boundary record shows plates moving apart and forming new crust, while another shows plates moving together and subducting crust. Which distinction between divergent boundaries and convergent boundaries matches the observations?
op: Divergent move together; convergent move apart
Divergent and convergent both move apart
Divergent and convergent both move together
Divergent move apart; convergent move together
mc.ex: Divergent boundaries move apart and form new crust, whereas convergent boundaries move together and can subduct crust. Assigning the motions in reverse swaps their supplied distinguishing relations.

mc.q: A review notation shows plates moving side by side, while a disputed label says divergent because crust is created. Under a deadline, which classification is supported by the recorded motion?
op: Transform moves together and subducts crust
Divergent separates plates and forms new crust
